name: Ancient Greek (Attic, active method)
ttsNote: There is no Ancient Greek voice. Audio uses the Modern Greek voice (Melina) with spelling adjusted toward reconstructed Attic: β δ γ as b d g, θ φ χ as t p k, η and ει as e, αι and οι as two vowels, υ as 'oo'. It can't do vowel length, aspiration or the pitch accent (it stresses the accented syllable instead). Use it as a rough guide.

chat.name: simple Attic Greek (active-method style; write with accents and breathings)

translit.name: Transliteration: ē/ō = long e/o (η, ω), kh/th/ph = k/t/p with a puff of air, h = rough breathing; accents mark the pitch accent

notes.title: How this pack works: reading first, active Greek
body: The goal is reading real Greek (Plato, Xenophon, the New Testament, Hippocrates) without a dictionary. As with Latin, the route is lots of easy Greek you understand, a little grammar at a time, and using the language actively: saying and writing simple sentences, and talking with Claude.
The readers are original, in the spirit of Rouse's direct-method *A Greek Boy at Home* (1909). From Unit 9 on you read authentic texts: a Hippocratic aphorism, Xenophon, Plato and the Gospel of John.
Each word gets a **reading card** (Greek sentence → meaning) and a **production card** (English → Greek).

notes.title: Reconstructed Attic pronunciation, briefly
body: This is how Athenians of Plato's time spoke, as reconstructed from spelling mistakes in inscriptions, ancient grammarians, Latin loans and animal noises in comedy (sheep say βῆ βῆ, so η was 'e', not Modern Greek 'i').

Key points: β γ δ are b g d; θ φ χ are t p k **with a puff of air** (as in English 'top, pot, cat'), while τ π κ have none (as in 'stop, spot, scat'); ζ is 'zd'; η is a long open e, ω a long open o; ει is a long closed e and ου a long u; υ is French u (lips rounded, say 'ee'); the rough breathing ( ῾ ) is h.
The accents mark **pitch**, not stress: acute = the voice rises, circumflex = rises and falls on a long vowel. Most learners stress the accented syllable; that's fine for now.
Modern Greek pronunciation differs a lot (β = v, η = i, θ = th). The audio here is a Modern Greek voice with respelling, so it can only approximate.

notes.title: Greek and Latin reinforce each other
body: You already know the hard part from Latin: **cases** (Greek has five: no ablative; its jobs go to the genitive and dative), agreement, and free word order. Shared concept pages (cases, dative, participles, aspect) explain each idea once for both languages.
New in Greek: the **article** ὁ ἡ τό ('the'), which Latin lacks; the **middle voice**; and many more **participles**, which Greek uses constantly.

Many words are Indo-European cousins of Latin ones (πατήρ / pater, ὄνομα / nōmen, φέρω / ferō, πούς / pēs), and English medicine is mostly Greek: cardiology, gastritis, pediatrics. Word cards show both.

notes.title: Unverified content
body: The Greek was written by Claude and checked against standard grammar, but not yet by a human Hellenist, so it is marked unverified. Accents in particular are easy to get slightly wrong. Tap ⚑ Flag error on anything that looks wrong. The authentic passages were typed from the standard texts and should be checked against Perseus.

scriptLessons.title: Letters 1: Α Β Γ Δ Ε Ζ
scriptLessons.note: Greek has 24 letters, most of which you half-know from math and science. Each has a capital and a small form; texts are written almost entirely in small letters.

letters.name: alpha
letters.sound: a as in 'father' (long) or 'idea' (short).

letters.name: bēta
letters.sound: b as in 'bed' (Modern Greek says v).

letters.name: gamma
letters.sound: Hard g as in 'get'. Before γ κ χ ξ it is 'ng': ἄγγελος = áng-gelos.

letters.name: delta
letters.sound: d as in 'dog'.

letters.name: e psīlón
letters.sound: Short e as in 'pet'.

letters.name: zēta
letters.sound: zd as in 'wisdom'.

scriptLessons.title: Letters 2: Η Θ Ι Κ Λ Μ
scriptLessons.note: Η is a vowel (long e), not h, and Θ is one sound.

letters.name: ēta
letters.sound: Long open e, like 'air' without the r. Sheep in Greek comedy say βῆ βῆ.

letters.name: thēta
letters.sound: t with a puff of air, as in 'top' (later and in Modern Greek: th as in 'thin').

letters.name: iōta
letters.sound: i as in 'machine' (long) or 'sit' (short).

letters.name: kappa
letters.sound: k without a puff of air, as in 'skin'.

letters.name: lambda
letters.sound: l as in 'let'.

letters.name: mū
letters.sound: m as in 'me'.

scriptLessons.title: Letters 3: Ν Ξ Ο Π Ρ Σ
scriptLessons.note: Watch out for false friends from the Latin alphabet: Ν ν is n, Ρ ρ is r, and small ν looks like a v.

letters.name: nū
letters.sound: n as in 'net'. Small ν looks like a v but is n.

letters.name: xeî
letters.sound: ks as in 'box'.

letters.name: o mīkrón
letters.sound: Short o, as in Spanish 'no' but short.

letters.name: peî
letters.sound: p without a puff of air, as in 'spin'.

letters.name: rhō
letters.sound: Rolled r as in Spanish 'perro'. At the start of a word it is breathy: ῥ = rh.

letters.name: sigma
letters.sound: s as in 'sun', never z. Written ς at the end of a word, σ elsewhere.

scriptLessons.title: Letters 4: Τ Υ Φ Χ Ψ Ω
scriptLessons.note: Φ and Χ are p and k with a puff of air in Attic; later Greek turned them into f and the German ch.

letters.name: tau
letters.sound: t without a puff of air, as in 'stop'.

letters.name: ŷ psīlón
letters.sound: French u: say 'ee' with rounded lips. In ου, αυ, ευ it is u.

letters.name: pheî
letters.sound: p with a puff of air, as in 'pot' (later f).

letters.name: kheî
letters.sound: k with a puff of air, as in 'cat' (later like German Bach).

letters.name: pseî
letters.sound: ps as in 'lapse'.

letters.name: ō méga
letters.sound: Long open o, as in 'awe'.

scriptLessons.title: Breathings, accents, diphthongs
scriptLessons.note: Every word starting with a vowel has a breathing mark; most words have one accent. Neither changes the letter.

letters.name: smooth and rough breathing
letters.sound: Over a first vowel (or ρ): ᾿ smooth = nothing; ῾ rough = h. ἡμέρα = hēmérā. On a diphthong it sits on the second vowel: οἱ = hoi.

letters.name: acute, grave, circumflex
letters.sound: Acute ´: the pitch rises. Circumflex ῀ (long vowels only): rises and falls. Grave `: replaces an acute on a last syllable before another word.

letters.name: diphthongs αι, οι
letters.sound: αι as in 'aisle', οι as in 'boy'.

letters.name: spellings ει, ου
letters.sound: Not diphthongs in Attic: ει is a long closed e (as in 'they' without the y), ου a long u as in 'food'.

letters.name: diphthongs αυ, ευ
letters.sound: αυ as in 'how'; ευ is e + u run together.

letters.name: iota subscript
letters.sound: A small ι under a long vowel: once pronounced (a long diphthong), silent in later Greek. Common in the dative: τῷ, τῇ.

letters.name: question mark and raised dot
letters.sound: The Greek question mark looks like our semicolon (;), and the raised dot (·) works like a colon or semicolon.

speaking.en: Introduce yourself in Greek: greet, give your name, say you're a student and how you are.
Say where five places are and whether they are big or small.
Describe your family: who is older, who is younger, whose child you are.
Say what you do always, often and never.
Describe a garden or campus, saying where things are with ἐν, ὑπό, εἰς, ἐκ.
Say who gives what to whom (dative).
Be the teacher: give five classroom commands.
Describe Athens or Baltimore: city, citizens, sea, day and night.
Tell a doctor what hurts, for how long, and ask what to do. You're pre-med: use the Greek behind the medical words.
Tell what you did yesterday, in order (aorist).
Retell the fable of the wolf and the lamb in your own words.
Read Xenophon's first sentence aloud, then explain it in simple Greek.
hints: Ὁ μὲν πρεσβύτερος …, ὁ δὲ νεώτερος …

scenarios.title: Meeting an Athenian student
scenarios.setup: You meet a student in the agora of Athens and introduce yourselves.

scenarios.title: Dinner in an Athenian house
scenarios.setup: An Athenian family invites you to dinner and asks about your family.
scenarios.partner: Aspasia, the mother of the house

scenarios.setup: You want to buy bread, wine and a book in the agora.

scenarios.title: Lost in Athens
scenarios.setup: You ask the way from the agora to the Acropolis and to the harbour (Piraeus).

scenarios.title: In class with a strict teacher
scenarios.setup: The teacher asks you questions about a story you read.

scenarios.title: At the Hippocratic doctor's
scenarios.setup: You have a headache and fever. The doctor, a student of Hippocrates, examines you and gives advice.

scenarios.title: What did you do yesterday?
scenarios.setup: A friend asks about your day yesterday.

scenarios.title: Telling a fable
scenarios.setup: Tell a child one of Aesop's fables and answer their questions about it.
